Peter Canisius
pē´tẽr ka-nĭsh´ĭ-ŭs
n. (Peter Canisius, 1521–1597, Dutch Jesuit, called the second apostle of Germany, whose catechisms and colleges recovered Austria and Bavaria for Rome)
Latinized from Dutch Pieter Kanis; Canisius plays on canis, a dog — the Dominicans' old pun, here attached to a Jesuit.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Peter Canisius was the first Dutchman to enter the Society of Jesus and spent forty years in Germany doing what the Protestants had done and Rome had not: catechizing. His Summa Doctrinae Christianae of 1555 and the two shorter catechisms that followed were printed in some four hundred editions in his lifetime, graded for scholars, children and the simple, in question and answer. He founded colleges at Vienna, Prague, Ingolstadt, Munich and Fribourg, preached, visited, and advised princes. He is the clearest proof that the Counter-Reformation was won in schoolrooms. The principle is Scripture's own and belongs to no party: “Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it” (Pro 22:6); “bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord” (Eph 6:4); and Psa 78:5, where God “established a testimony in Jacob…that they should make them known to their children.” What was taught in those books was Trent, and so the method was right and the content was the error.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a catechism as a form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.

expand to see more

CAT'ECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.

2. An elementary book containing a summary of principles in any science or art, but appropriately in religion, reduced to the form of questions and answers.

CAT'ECHIZE, v.t. To instruct by asking questions, receiving answers, and offering explanations and corrections.

Key Scripture

Pro 22:6 — "Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it."

Eph 6:4 — "And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord."

Psa 78:5 — "For he established a testimony in Jacob, and appointed a law in Israel, which he commanded our fathers, that they should make them known to their children:"

Mat 18:6 — "But whoso shall offend one of these little ones which believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea."

Modern Corruption

Canisius beat the Protestants at catechizing, and the lesson for a Reformed church is about the method before it is about the man.

expand to see more

The Reformation began with catechisms — Luther's Small Catechism, the Heidelberg, the Genevan, later the Westminster Shorter and the Baptist Catechism — and wherever it stopped using them it lost ground. Canisius understood that a generation is held by whoever teaches its children, and he out-worked the Lutherans in their own territories. Pro 22:6 and Eph 6:4 are not denominational property; the household and the church that neglect them will lose their children to whoever does not. The sharpest rebuke a Reformed reader can take from this entry is that a Jesuit took the family and the schoolroom more seriously than many Protestants then or now.

The content is the other half, and it must be named. The doctrine those four hundred editions carried was Trent's: justification by infused righteousness increased by merit, seven sacraments, the invocation of saints, purgatory, the Mass as a propitiatory sacrifice. Mat 18:6 is a terrible word about what is taught to little ones — “whoso shall offend one of these little ones which believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck.” Method without truth is efficient harm. The recovery is to catechize as diligently as Canisius did, out of a confession that is scriptural.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chanak (H2596), to train, to dedicate; Greek paideia (G3809), nurture, instruction; nouthesia (G3559), admonition.

Hebrew chanak (H2596) — to train up, to dedicate; Proverbs 22:6.

Greek paideia (G3809) — nurture, training of a child; Ephesians 6:4.

Greek nouthesia (G3559) — admonition, warning; Ephesians 6:4.

Hebrew eduth (H5715) — a testimony; Psalm 78:5.

Greek skandalizo (G4624) — to cause to stumble, to offend; Matthew 18:6.

Usage

"“Train up a child in the way he should go” (Pro 22:6) — the method he mastered."

"“bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord” (Eph 6:4) — the charge to households."

"“whoso shall offend one of these little ones” (Mat 18:6) — the weight of what is taught them."
